newsitem.title: UK: Buba's Jochimsen - hardest part of EMU may be later.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Jochimsen - hardest part of EMU may be later.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said on Wednesday the hardest part of a single currency might come after it is set up and he urged quasi- automatic penalties to prevent backsliding by member states.
"The start of EMU may be child's play compared with the integration achievements needed by fiscal, social and other policies after the union has started," Jochimsen told Reuters Financial Television.

Jochimsen, who was in London for a conference, stressed that countries had to meet all of the Maastricht criteria in a sustainable way and not just as a one-off achievement "glued together and reached more or less by chance".

Jochimsen advocated "quasi-automatic sanctions" for EMU members that breached the terms of a proposed stability pact intended to prevent economies from drifting away from Maastricht criteria after the union was set up.

If such penalties were left to discretionary political decisions when problems cropped up, this could mean six different votes in the European Union Council of Ministers before countries could be penalised.
Such a "cumbersome, worn-out" process was open to political opportunism that could damage EMU's credibility.
Jochimsen said the drive to curb the deficits of EU member states would be needed even without EMU.

Although the timetable to achieve the criteria for EMU was producing "quality pressure" on member states, it would be up to EU government leaders in two years to decide whether the start of EMU would have to be postponed.
Jochimsen cautioned against relaxing the Maastricht criteria for a single currency although he said accelerating moves toward economic integration risked sparking social unrest.
"The criteria are more important than a timely start (to European Economic and Monetary Union)", he said.
Jochimsen said the question of social unrest might come up in some countries due to the speed of integration efforts needed to make up for lost time.
"I cannot help this. It is a problem which the political setup will have to solve in the different countries."
Jochimsen said British entry into EMU as a founder member would be "very desirable".
"We may have differences but we have many similarities," he said, adding that Britain shared an interest in ensuring the stability of the single market.
